statement: In three healthy Japanese men who received five racemic ketamine preparations at least a week apart, measured against the same men's intravenous curves, about 32% of a sublingual tablet reached the bloodstream (32.2%, SD 8.2, and 32.1%, SD 7.2 for the two mirror-image forms), about 29 to 31% of a suppository (28.9%, SD 18.9, and 30.8%, SD 30.6) and about 44 to 46% of a nasal spray (43.8%, SD 11.4, and 46.4%, SD 12.9), the highest figure of the preparations tested (Yanagihara et al., 2003). Peak levels were between 29.3 and 61.6 ng/mL at about 17 to 40 minutes, and the metabolite norketamine was formed least after the nasal spray (area 115.9 and 100.7 ng·h/mL against 533.8 and 494.9 after the swallowed tablet, although the nasal pair is headed as the area to 8 hours in the table and called the area to 6 hours in the abstract and the discussion, because norketamine was below the detection limit 8 hours after the spray, so the two are not measured over the same window). Each figure is the mean of three men. Two of the conditions did not deliver what their names say: the men swallowed the sublingual tablets with saliva, so that condition was partly gastrointestinal, and not all of them had a bowel preparation before the suppository, which the authors give as the reason the rectal values varied so much that the spread is about the size of the figure itself. The study was open, the order of the five sessions is not described, no test statistic is printed, no elimination half-life is given for any of these preparations, and the two times to peak printed for the nasal spray cannot be means of three measurements taken at the sampling times the paper lists. A 2016 review nonetheless carries the rectal (about 30%) and nasal (about 45%) figures forward in its text, second-hand and without the sample size of three, which it prints only in its table. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: A small study gave three men ketamine in different forms, one at a time. Compared with an injection into a vein, about 45 in every 100 parts of a nasal spray reached the blood, about 30 in 100 of a tablet under the tongue and about 30 in 100 of a suppository. Only three men took part, the men swallowed the tablets that were meant to stay under the tongue, and the suppository figures varied enormously between them. The study says nothing about how long the drug lasted after these forms.
population: Three healthy Japanese men aged 27 to 40 and weighing 60 to 72 kg, each receiving all five preparations
exposure: A single racemic ketamine preparation (study conditions: two sublingual tablets containing 25 mg each, one suppository containing 50 mg, and an aqueous solution containing 25 mg given by nasal atomizer, each at least a week apart)
comparator: A 20 mg intravenous injection in the same men as the reference for absolute availability
outcome: Share of the dose reaching the bloodstream, peak level and time to peak, and norketamine exposure
magnitude: Bioavailability, (R)- then (S)-enantiomer: sublingual tablet 32.2% (SD 8.2) and 32.1% (SD 7.2); suppository 28.9% (SD 18.9) and 30.8% (SD 30.6); nasal spray 43.8% (SD 11.4) and 46.4% (SD 12.9); swallowed tablet 18.3% (SD 4.7) and 17.6% (SD 3.8) in the same men. Peaks 61.6 (SD 21.3) and 56.9 (SD 22.8) ng/mL at 40.0 and 36.7 min sublingual, 42.8 (SD 31.1) and 38.8 (SD 30.2) at 23.3 min rectal, 29.4 (SD 16.5) and 29.3 (SD 13.8) at 22.5 and 17.5 min nasal. Norketamine area 115.9 and 100.7 ng·h/mL nasal (headed as the area to 8 hours in Table 2, called the area to 6 hours in the abstract and the Discussion) against 533.8 and 494.9 to 8 hours after the swallowed tablet. n = 3 for every figure.

evidence.locator: Table 1, sublingual tablet, suppository and nasal spray rows (columns Cmax, Tmax and BA)
evidence.extracted: Against the same men's intravenous curves, (R)- then (S)-enantiomer: sublingual tablet bioavailability 32.2% (SD 8.2) and 32.1% (SD 7.2), peak 61.6 (SD 21.3) and 56.9 (SD 22.8) ng/mL at 40.0 (SD 20.0) and 36.7 (SD 20.8) min; suppository 28.9% (SD 18.9) and 30.8% (SD 30.6), peak 42.8 (SD 31.1) and 38.8 (SD 30.2) ng/mL at 23.3 (SD 5.7) min; nasal spray 43.8% (SD 11.4) and 46.4% (SD 12.9), peak 29.4 (SD 16.5) and 29.3 (SD 13.8) ng/mL at 22.5 (SD 9.6) and 17.5 (SD 5.0) min. The half-life column is filled only for the injection row.

The text rounds the same figures: bioavailability approximately 20% for the tablet and 30% for the sublingual tablet and the suppository, and approximately 45% for the nasal spray, the highest value of the preparations tested. Ketamine was detected 5 to 20 minutes after each of these preparations, mean maximum concentrations of 30 to 50 ng/mL came at 20 to 30 minutes, and concentrations were below the detection limit by 4 to 6 hours; the detection limit itself is never stated.

evidence.locator: Table 2, column AUC(0→8h); the interpretation in the Discussion paragraph beginning on p. 42
evidence.extracted: Norketamine exposure in three healthy men, (R)- then (S)-enantiomer: 533.8 and 494.9 ng·h/mL after the swallowed tablet, 462.9 and 408.7 after the sublingual tablet, 322.6 and 282.6 after the suppository, 173.8 and 149.8 after the injection, and 115.9 and 100.7 after the nasal spray. The nasal pair is headed as the area to 8 hours in Table 2 but called the area to 6 hours in the abstract and the Discussion, because norketamine was below the detection limit 8 hours after the spray, so that pair is integrated over a shorter window than the other four. The reading that the nasal route largely escapes first-pass metabolism is the authors', stated in the Discussion on p. 42, not in the table.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (left column) and 2nd paragraph (right column)
evidence.extracted: The men swallowed the sublingual tablets using saliva, so part of that condition was absorption from the gut; in a preliminary comparison, not swallowing saliva for an hour lowered the one-hour area and the peak by 35 to 50%, with the number of participants not reported. The authors attribute the large variation in the rectal values to differences in absorption, because not all of the men had a rectal enema before the suppository was inserted.

evidence.locator: Methods › Sampling and analysis (p. 38); Table 1, nasal spray row, column Tmax (p. 41)
evidence.extracted: Blood was taken before dosing and at 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 minutes and at 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 hours, all multiples of five minutes, so the printed nasal times to peak of 22.5 (SD 9.6) and 17.5 (SD 5.0) minutes cannot be means of three such measurements; the nasal row is the one the later clinical review cites for nasal bioavailability.

evidence.locator: Sections 7.4 Sublingual Ketamine, 7.5 Nasal Ketamine and 7.6 Rectal Ketamine
evidence.extracted: The review states, second-hand, that sublingual and oral ketamine share a bioavailability of 24 to 30%, that nasal bioavailability is approximately 45% with peaks reached in 10 to 17 minutes and low norketamine exposure, and that rectal bioavailability is approximately 30% with a norketamine area very similar to the sublingual one, citing this three-person study for the rectal and nasal figures; it adds that the amount given nasally is difficult to control.

evidence.locator: Table 1, the five rows citing [12]: Keta iv 20 mg, Keta po 50 mg, Keta sl 50 mg, Keta pr 50 mg and Keta in 25 mg, with footnotes c and d (pp. 4-5); Sections 7.5 Nasal Ketamine and 7.6 Rectal Ketamine (p. 13)
evidence.extracted: The review's own table prints n = 3 for each of the five preparations of the 2003 study, next to the same peak, time-to-peak and area values as the primary paper (for example the nasal row: peak 29.4 (SD 16.5) and 29.3 (SD 13.8) ng/mL at 22.5 (SD 9.6) and 17.5 (SD 5.0) minutes, norketamine areas 115.9 (SD 17.6) and 100.7 (SD 39.6) ng·h/mL), with a footnote recording that the norketamine areas run from baseline to 8 hours. The bioavailability column of the table is empty for all five rows, so the figures the review's text gives for the rectal and nasal routes appear only in that text, without the sample size the table carries.

risk_of_bias.note: Open administration with no randomization, counterbalancing or order described; two conditions did not deliver what their labels say (sublingual tablets swallowed with saliva, suppositories without a standard bowel preparation); no test statistic, interval or individual value for any of seventy tabulated numbers; the assay's detection limit is never stated although conclusions rest on it (card sc_yanagihara_2003, overall high).

inconsistency.note: One study; no second measurement of any of these preparations in the sources read here.

indirectness.note: The preparations were measured directly; but the tablet and suppository were made by the authors' own group, so the figures describe those preparations, not every sublingual, rectal or nasal product.

imprecision.note: Three men, so every figure moves a third if one man is unusual; for the suppository the standard deviation is about the size of the mean (28.9%, SD 18.9; 30.8%, SD 30.6).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from one small primary study.

grade.reasoning: A within-person crossover with an intravenous reference starts high (METHODS §6.3), but this one is open and unrandomized, two conditions were not delivered as labelled, and nothing is reported with a test statistic or an interval: risk of bias −2. Imprecision −1 for three men with standard deviations approaching the means. Very low, which is the floor. These are nevertheless the figures the 2016 review carries as the rectal and nasal bioavailability of ketamine, which is why the claim names their sample size.
